biography: Most of Plato's dialogues are set in the Periclean period; Russell reads Plato's picture of leisured, wealthy young men absorbed in mathematics and philosophy as reflecting Plato's own aristocratic upbringing, before war and democracy eroded that class's wealth and security. Presented by Russell as the chief source, and chief critic, of the Sophists, caricaturing and vilifying them (e.g. in the Euthydemus, the Sophist, the Protagoras, the Theaetetus, the Republic, the Gorgias); Russell accuses Plato of intellectual dishonesty, twisting arguments toward conclusions he judges virtuous rather than following them wherever they lead. Socrates's other principal pupil and Russell's main source, especially via the Apology, which Russell treats as broadly historical in intent though not a verbatim transcript; Russell notes the difficulty of distinguishing the historical Socrates from a mouthpiece for Plato's own views in the later dialogues. Named as the philosopher most decisively shaped by the Spartan myth; the chapter closes by promising the next chapter will detail Sparta's effect on his Utopia (the Republic). The chapter's subject: Russell surveys the biographical and philosophical influences (Pythagoras, Parmenides, Heraclitus, Socrates) that shaped his political and metaphysical outlook, and states his intent to treat Plato 'with as little reverence as if he were a contemporary English or American advocate of totalitarianism.' Primary subject: Russell reconstructs, in detail, the ideal city set out in the Republic (through Book V and the definition of justice in Book IV), including its class structure, education, eugenics, communism, and 'noble lie,' and subjects Plato's definition of justice to sustained criticism. Primary subject: Russell reconstructs Plato's definition of the philosopher, the knowledge/opinion distinction, the theory of Ideas (logical and metaphysical parts), the divided line, the allegory of the cave, the role of the Good, and the guardian curriculum, from Republic Books V-VII. Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the Phaedo's dramatic frame, Plato's soul/body dualism, his account of the philosophic life as a preparation for death, and the three arguments Plato has Socrates give for immortality (from opposites, from recollection, from simplicity), together with his account of transmigration. Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the Timaeus's account of creation, the four elements and their geometric structure, the nature of time and space, the two souls in man, and the doctrine of transmigration, using the Pythagorean character Timaeus as Plato's mouthpiece. Author of the Theaetetus; Russell examines his critique of the definition 'knowledge is perception,' his handling of Protagorean relativism and Heraclitean flux, and his final argument that knowledge requires apprehending existence, likeness, and number, none of which is perceived through any sense-organ. Constant point of comparison; Russell describes Aristotle's metaphysics as 'Plato diluted by common sense,' and traces how far Aristotle's doctrines of universals and form remain covertly Platonic despite his explicit criticisms of the theory of Ideas. Named as the source of the tripartite division of the soul (rational and irrational, the latter further divided into vegetative and appetitive) that Aristotle adopts, and as holding the more mystical, ascetic view of pleasure that Aristotle's more moderate treatment implicitly corrects. His Republic is criticized at length by Aristotle (as reported by Russell) for giving the State too much unity, for the proposed abolition of the family, and for communism of property; Russell judges these to be among Aristotle's more persuasive arguments. Revered by Plotinus above all other philosophers (referred to simply as 'He'); Plotinus draws mainly on the theory of Forms/ideas, the mystical passages of the Phaedo and Republic Book VI, and the discussion of love in the Symposium, while leaving out Plato's political interests, dramatic character portraits, mathematics, and playfulness -- producing what Russell calls a less 'full-blooded' Plato than the original. Cited as holding, with Aristotle, that God is an 'artificer' who imposes form on eternal, pre-existing matter rather than a true Creator; also praised at length by Augustine in Book VIII of The City of God as the greatest of the philosophers, nearest to Christianity on God and immortality. Named by Boethius, along with Socrates and Aristotle, as one of the 'true philosophers,' as against the Stoics and Epicureans, whom Boethius regards as usurpers of philosophy's name; the Consolation is described by Russell as purely Platonic in its metaphysics. Cited as an example of pre-individualist Greek thought: his Republic is concerned with defining the good community, not the good individual. Cited as an opponent of the identification of knowledge with perception (in the Theaetetus) and, with Descartes and the scholastics, as a target of Locke's Book I attack on innate ideas. Criticized by Nietzsche for their supposed democratic moral bias and taste for edification; Nietzsche cannot forgive Socrates his humble origin, calling him a 'roturier,' and suggests Plato may have preached virtue only as a means of controlling the lower classes.
central_doctrines: The Spartan reality vs. the Spartan myth: Russell's distinction between Sparta's factual institutions and conduct (documented critically by Aristotle and others) and the romanticized 'myth,' chiefly transmitted by Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus, which most profoundly influenced political theory from Plato onward. The four philosophical sources of Plato's authoritarianism: Russell's argument that Plato's politics follow from combining (a) Pythagoras's religious other-worldliness and mathematical mysticism, (b) Parmenides's doctrine that reality is timeless and change illusory, (c) Heraclitus's doctrine (combined with Parmenides) that sense knowledge is unreliable, and (d) Socrates's ethical focus on 'the Good,' yielding the view that the best state is the one that most nearly copies a timeless, perfect model and is ruled by those who understand that eternal Good. The problem of political 'wisdom': Russell's two-part critical question: first, whether there is a generalized political 'wisdom' (distinct from specialized skills like shoemaking or medicine) consisting in knowledge of the good; second, whether any constitutional arrangement (aristocracy, monarchy, educational credentialing) can reliably select for and empower such wisdom. The three-class Utopia (guardians, soldiers, producers): Plato's tripartite social structure in which political authority is restricted to a numerically small guardian class (chosen initially by the legislator, thereafter mainly hereditary, with exceptional promotion or demotion based on merit), a larger soldier class enforcing the guardians' will, and the mass of common people engaged in productive labor. Communism of property and of the family: Plato's proposal that the guardian (and possibly soldier) class hold all property in common, live communally like a military camp, and abolish private marriage and parenthood: 'breeding' festivals are rigged by the rulers under cover of a lottery to concentrate reproduction among the 'best' individuals, all children are removed at birth and raised collectively, and kinship terms (father, mother, brother, sister) are extended loosely by age-cohort to preserve social taboos without genetic tracking. The 'noble lie' (myth of the metals): A government-sanctioned foundational myth (the 'one royal lie'), asserting citizens are born of different divinely ordained metals corresponding to their social class, intended to be believed by nearly the entire population (rulers possibly excepted) and sustained across generations through education. Plato's definition of justice: The Republic's culminating definition (reached in Book IV): justice consists in each class, and each individual, doing its own proper work without interference in the work of others, an idea Russell connects to an older Greek notion (traceable to Anaximander) of each thing having its 'appointed place and function,' violation of which constitutes hubris to be cosmically punished. Ethical objectivism vs. Thrasymachean relativism (the status of 'the Good'): The debate, launched by Thrasymachus's claim that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger,' over whether ethical statements have objective truth-value independent of desire and power, or whether, absent such objectivity, ethical disagreement reduces to contests of force or propaganda. Knowledge versus opinion: Plato's epistemic distinction, argued in Republic Book V, that knowledge (infallible, because it is logically impossible to know what is not) is of the eternal, unchanging Forms, while opinion (fallible, since particular sensible objects combine opposite characters and are thus intermediate between being and not-being) is of the world presented to the senses. The Theory of Ideas (Forms): Plato's doctrine, partly logical and partly metaphysical, that general words signify not particular things but a single, timeless, non-spatial universal nature ('cattyness,' the Idea of Beauty, the Idea of Bed) in which particulars 'participate' imperfectly; the metaphysical elaboration adds that each Idea is a single perfect object created by God. The Allegory of the Cave: Plato's extended simile (Republic Book VII) in which prisoners bound in an underground den, seeing only firelit shadows on a wall, represent ordinary humanity confined to sense-perception and opinion; escape into sunlight represents the philosopher's ascent, through dialectic, to knowledge of the Ideas and ultimately of the Good. The Idea of the Good: In Plato's scheme, the Good occupies a position higher than mere 'essence' or being; it is the source both of the reality of the other Ideas and of the mind's power to know them, and dialectic culminates in its direct perception, thereby dispensing with the hypotheses required by mathematics. Soul-body dualism: Plato's metaphysical pairing, in the Phaedo, of soul with reality/ideas/reason and body with appearance/sensible-objects/sense-perception, in which the first term of each pair is superior in both reality and goodness to the second, with death defined as the soul's separation from the body. The theory of recollection (anamnesis): The doctrine that all a priori knowledge (especially mathematical and logical concepts such as absolute equality, which is never actually found among sensible objects) is recollection of knowledge the soul possessed in a prior, disembodied existence, developed in the Phaedo and at greater length in the Meno via the interrogation of an untutored slave-boy about geometry. The argument from simplicity: Plato's argument that dissolution presupposes composition, that the soul (unlike the body) is simple and akin in nature to the unchanging essences it is capable of contemplating, and therefore, like those essences, cannot begin, end, or change -- and so must be classified among eternal things. Creation as ordering of pre-existing chaos: The Timaeus's account of the Demiurge (Creator) as a craftsman-God who, being good and without jealousy, imposes mathematical order and proportion on already-existing, chaotically moving material, modeling the resulting world as closely as possible on the eternal archetype apprehended by reason. The four elements and geometric atomism: Timaeus's theory that the four sensible elements are composed, at a deeper level, of two types of right triangle (half-square and half-equilateral), which combine into the faces of four of the five regular (Platonic) solids, with each element identified with a particular solid; the fifth solid, the dodecahedron, cannot be built from these triangles and is instead associated by Plato with the universe as a whole. Time as 'the moving image of eternity': Plato's account of time as a created 'moving image of eternity,' proceeding 'according to number,' brought into existence simultaneously with the heavens, such that strictly speaking one should say only 'is' of eternal being, while 'was' and 'will be' properly apply to the created, temporal image of eternity.

russell_view: Russell justifies devoting unusually extensive treatment to Plato (and, to a lesser extent, Aristotle) on the grounds that Plato was the more influential of the two most influential philosophers in Western history, partly because Aristotle himself grew out of Plato and partly because early Christian theology was more Platonic than Aristotelian. He then explains Plato's turn toward authoritarian politics through both biography (aristocratic birth, family ties to the Thirty Tyrants, the trauma of Athens's defeat, and the execution of his teacher Socrates by the democracy) and philosophical inheritance (Pythagoras, Parmenides, Heraclitus, and Socrates). Russell draws out four specific logical links between this inheritance and Plato's authoritarianism: the timelessness of the Good implying a static ideal state; the incommunicable, quasi-mystical certainty of Plato's core beliefs, echoing a Pythagorean 'rule of the initiate'; the heavy mathematical education this requires, implying oligarchy; and the assumption that leisure (available only to the wealthy) is necessary for wisdom. Russell states plainly that his own aim, unlike most commentators, is to understand Plato while treating him 'with as little reverence as if he were a contemporary English or American advocate of totalitarianism.' He closes the chapter by posing two general questions about political wisdom and concluding that no constitution can reliably identify and empower the wise, which he calls 'the ultimate reason for democracy.'
why_this_matters: Russell treats Plato as the single most influential philosopher in Western history, more so even than Aristotle, partly because early Christian thought was more Platonic than Aristotelian.
